column5: sun's ordered course through the gates
column6: The commentary's source gloss pictures stars swimming in their courses; the Astronomical Book lays out the sun's recurring course through the heavenly gates, adding a Jewish account of ordered celestial motion without equating it with swimming.

column5: luminaries depart their appointed courses
column6: The commentary gives the stars an ordered orbit; Enoch's vision associates a sinful age with celestial lights departing their appointed order, preserving a contrary image in which the course itself fails.

column5: water deep enough to swim in
column6: The commentary gives س ب ح the literal gloss “swim in water”; Ezekiel's temple river grows until it is deep enough for swimming, adding a sacred, measured current as a concrete water-motion image.

column5: stately stride
column6: The commentary's yusr gloss praises an animal's well-transferred steps; Proverbs calls several creatures stately in their going, making dignified gait itself the point rather than speed.

column5: separated herds in a moving caravan
column6: The commentary arranges horses and camels by those ahead and behind; Jacob sends successive animal droves ahead with space between them, adding a staged caravan whose order serves a plan.

column5: Arabic source root ء خ ر and Hebrew אחרית, latter end
column6: The commentary labels 87:17's Arabic al-ākhirah with the root ء خ ر and describes what remains behind; Moses recalls wilderness testing intended to do Israel good at its אחרית, its latter end, giving the cognate a delayed-benefit context.

column5: Arabic source root ء خ ر and Hebrew אחור, behind
column6: The commentary uses the Arabic root for both the afterlife and those at the rear; the psalm says God encompasses the speaker “behind and before,” showing the Hebrew cognate's spatial sense alongside the source's temporal one.

column5: Arabic source al-ākhirah and Hebrew אחרית, future
column6: The commentary says the Arabic “after/latter” names those at a group's end; the psalm uses Hebrew אחרית for the peaceful person's future, adding an ethical outcome to the cognate's temporal sense.

column5: brief pain, ever-flowing life
column6: The commentary contrasts the near life with what lasts afterward; the final brother says those who endured brief suffering have entered ever-flowing life, making the short/lasting contrast explicit in a martyr's speech.

column5: awakening to everlasting life
column6: The commentary says the later life is better and more enduring; Daniel describes sleepers in the dust awakening, some to everlasting life, supplying an explicit resurrection horizon.

column5: rest, then rise at the end of days
column6: The commentary makes the afterlife the latter stage and calls it lasting; Daniel is told to go to his rest and rise for his allotted inheritance at the end of days, giving that sequence a personal resurrection outcome.

column5: Moses completes a written book
column6: The commentary says the message is in earlier scrolls and names Moses; Deuteronomy says Moses finishes writing the words of the Torah in a book, a concrete Mosaic witness to written scripture.

column5: book of the law deposited as witness
column6: The commentary names Moses among the sources of the earlier scrolls; Moses orders the written book of the law placed beside the covenant ark as a witness, adding its preserved public role.

column5: World to Come beyond rivalry
column6: The commentary extends a race's front and rear positions to the afterlife; Berakhot portrays the World to Come without eating, trade, jealousy, hatred, or competition, with the righteous enjoying God's presence, limiting the race image to this life's sequence.

column5: thanksgiving and calling on God's name
column6: The commentary says the worshipper remembers the Lord's name and prays; the psalm joins a thanksgiving offering with calling on YHWH's name, adding a concrete liturgical form of that pairing.

column5: the present age and the future age
column6: The commentary contrasts the near life with the better, lasting life after it; in chapter 7 Uriel compares the hard passage of the present age with the future age's reward. Verse divisions vary by edition, so this is cited at chapter level.

column5: birthright exchanged for one meal
column6: The commentary condemns preferring the near life over what follows; Esau trades his birthright for food and despises it, a concrete choice of immediate satisfaction over a later inheritance.

column5: Esau sells inheritance for a meal
column6: The commentary's 87:16–17 contrast is immediate preference against later good; Hebrews names Esau as one who sold his birthright for a single meal, turning the Genesis episode into an ethical warning about short-term choice.

column5: later regret cannot recover the blessing
column6: The commentary says the early choice may not win the final outcome; Hebrews recalls that Esau later sought the blessing with tears but could not reverse what happened, adding the consequence of a short-sighted exchange.

column5: Abraham's company desires a better country
column6: The commentary names Abraham in the former scrolls and says the later life is better; Hebrews says the patriarchs desired a better, heavenly country, making Abrahamic faith look beyond the present homeland.

column5: Moses rejects fleeting pleasure
column6: The commentary criticizes preferring this world's life; Hebrews says Moses chose mistreatment with God's people over the temporary enjoyment of sin, a direct choice against near pleasure.

column5: Moses looks toward the reward
column6: The commentary says what follows is better than the first gain; Hebrews says Moses valued reproach above Egypt's treasures because he looked toward the reward, making future recompense govern present choice.

column5: Moses' writing read as forward-looking
column6: The commentary says the message is in former scrolls and names Moses; Jesus says Moses wrote about him, a New Testament interpretation that gives Mosaic scripture a forward-looking witness.

column5: losing present life to keep eternal life
column6: The commentary says people prefer worldly life over the better later one; Jesus says one who loves life loses it, while one who gives up life in this world keeps it for eternal life, directly reversing that preference.

column5: prayer begins by hallowing the Father's name
column6: The commentary says the worshipper remembers the Lord's name and then prays; Jesus teaches prayer that opens by asking that the Father's name be hallowed, joining divine-name devotion to the prayer itself.

column5: last and first at the kingdom's table
column6: The commentary says the first arrival is not necessarily the winner; after describing entry into God's kingdom, Jesus says some who are last will be first and first last, placing the reversal in an eschatological gathering.

column5: endurance to the end
column6: The commentary's horse holds strength for the latter stretch; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved, making final persistence decisive.

column5: discipline or risk disqualification
column6: The commentary says an early position does not guarantee the final win; Paul disciplines his body lest, after preaching to others, he himself be disqualified, adding the possibility that even a runner can fail at the end.

column5: athlete crowned only under the rules
column6: The commentary links the race order to a later prize; Paul says an athlete is not crowned unless competing lawfully, adding that position and desire alone do not secure the outcome.

column5: rich urged not to hope in uncertain wealth
column6: The commentary says people prefer worldly life; Paul tells the rich not to set hope on uncertain wealth but on God, a specific correction to misplaced present security.

column5: treasure stored for the future life
column6: The commentary calls the later life better and lasting; Paul says the rich should store up treasure as a foundation for the future and take hold of the life that is truly life, spelling out present action for future gain.

column5: crown of life after endurance
column6: The commentary says the horse preserves its running for later; James blesses the one who endures trial and promises the crown of life, making the reward follow sustained endurance.

column5: imperishable inheritance reserved in heaven
column6: The commentary says the afterlife is more enduring; Peter describes an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven, adding a reserved future possession.

column5: earthly residence, heavenly citizenship
column6: The commentary treats this life as an earlier position before the lasting life; Diognetus describes Christians as dwelling on earth while their citizenship is in heaven, giving the temporal contrast the image of temporary residence versus permanent homeland.
